title: Overview
subtitle: Kevin McCalley — Senior Front-End Engineer & UI/UX Designer

content.text: I design and build **accessible, responsive web applications** — from Figma prototype through to shipped, maintained product. My core is visual design and front-end engineering in **React** and **TypeScript**; over the last few years I've extended that into **full-stack delivery**: API design, relational data modeling, authentication, payments, and deployment.

I've shipped and now operate several production applications end to end, including **AccessBridge**, an automated WCAG / ADA auditing platform, and **Groundswell**, a global surf-forecasting service. That same end-to-end approach also drives **GoodStockPress**, a line of 18 personalized print-on-demand card decks — each its own browser-based personalization wizard — sold on Etsy. **AI-assisted development** (Claude) is part of my daily workflow — I use it to move faster while keeping architecture, code review, and accountability firmly with me.

Skilled communicator with a track record of translating complex requirements into accessible, maintainable interfaces — and, increasingly, the systems behind them. Comfortable owning a feature from design file to production.
• **Languages & Frameworks:** React, TypeScript, JavaScript (ES6+), Node.js, HTML5, CSS3, SCSS; Next.js, Hono, Express
• **UI & Design:** Figma, Adobe XD, Photoshop, Illustrator, Framer Motion, Tailwind CSS, Material UI
• **Back End & Data:** PostgreSQL (Neon), Drizzle ORM, SQLite, REST API design, background jobs & scheduled tasks
• **Platform & Tooling:** Vercel, Railway, Git, Vite, npm / pnpm, Stripe, Clerk / OAuth, Playwright, axe-core, Postman, Jira, Confluence

title: How I Work
subtitle: Design judgment, held steady through a much faster process.

content.text: My process has changed more in the last two years than in the ten before them. Most of a build now happens in structured dialogue with an AI collaborator: I describe what an interface needs to do and how it should feel, we work through it in passes, and the work is tracked on a living checklist we close out item by item. It is faster than the Figma-to-handoff cycle it replaced, and — to my own surprise — more fluid. What has not moved is where the judgment sits.

• **Taste is the constraint, not the tool.** Layout, hierarchy, typography, motion, what to leave out — those calls are still mine. AI widens how much I can try and how quickly; it does not decide what is good.

• **The work is specified, not just prompted.** Every build runs against an explicit artifact — a scoped checklist of what finished means for each piece — so progress stays legible and honest about what is actually done.
• **I own what ships.** Architecture, review, and accountability stay with me. The speed comes from cutting time on the mechanical parts, not from skipping the parts that matter.
Recent end-to-end product work — design, front end, back end, and infrastructure. Each was built solo, shipped to production, and is maintained live.

items.name: AccessBridge
items.tagline: Automated WCAG / ADA accessibility audits for small-business sites
items.description: A real-browser scanner (axe-core + Playwright) that renders every page, catches the violations static checkers miss, and returns a prioritized, plain-language fix guide. Full SaaS: authentication, subscription billing, usage metering, and a background job queue.
items.scope: Sole developer — design, front end, API, database, deployment

items.name: Groundswell
items.tagline: Honest global surf forecasting with a published accuracy record
items.description: Surf and swell forecasts for 600+ spots worldwide, refreshed every few hours, backed by 4+ years of historical data and a public scorecard that grades its own past predictions. Installable PWA, five languages, tiered subscriptions.
items.scope: Sole developer — product, UI, data pipeline, i18n, billing

items.name: S&P Daily
items.tagline: A deterministic, self-grading daily S&P 500 forecast
items.description: Each trading morning a scheduled job collects ~9 groups of market data, scores them with pure math (no LLM), classifies a market regime, and stores a probabilistic next-day forecast. After the close a second job grades it — direction, error, Brier score — so the system is falsifiable rather than an "AI horoscope."
items.scope: Sole developer — data collectors, factor engine, evaluator, dashboard

items.name: GoodStockPress
items.tagline: An 18-product line of personalized, print-at-home card decks — each its own browser-based personalization wizard
items.description: Digital-download card decks and stationery sold on Etsy — affirmation decks, tribute decks, kids' trading cards, wedding suites — each personalized in a short web wizard that scores quiz answers against a hand-written content bank (or takes real names and photos), then renders a print-ready, multi-page PDF entirely in the browser with jsPDF, along with Cricut / Silhouette cut files. A shared hub site adds a searchable catalogue, a blog, and a serverless print-shop finder. Built deliberately dependency-light — no framework, no build step.
items.scope: Sole developer — product design, content banks, in-browser PDF engine, hub site, SEO

items.name: Acrylic Mix Lab
items.tagline: OKLab colour solver for mixing acrylic paint
items.description: Enter a target colour and the app solves for the parts-by-weight recipe from your actual tube set, working in perceptually-uniform OKLab space. Saved recipes, tube calibration, and a custom-paint library.

items.name: LunchLanguage
items.tagline: A language-learning game for kids — cook a meal, then solve math puzzles about it
items.description: Kids pick a meal, drag ingredients to build it, then answer math questions about what they made. The whole game — Chef Zesty's dialogue, menus, and quiz — is localized into nine languages with an in-game language picker, so a child can play through it in a language they're learning. Fully client-side and animation-driven, with my own kids as product testers.

items.name: Translate App
items.tagline: A personal translation workspace — phrasebooks, flashcards, and PDF export
items.description: Translates text between six languages with text-to-speech playback, a built-in common-phrases book, and user-defined phrase lists that can be drilled as themed flashcards or exported to PDF. A post-processing pass rewrites Brazilian Portuguese output into European Portuguese from a hand-built substitution dictionary. Client-only React app with a Material UI interface and a switchable theme system.

title: Case Study
subtitle: Groundswell — honest surf forecasting with a public accuracy record.

steps.label: The problem
steps.body: Every surf-forecast site shows you a swell chart; none show you how often the chart was right. Surfers plan dawn patrols and whole trips around numbers they have no way to audit, from services that never grade themselves.

steps.label: The bet
steps.body: Build the forecast **and** the scorecard. Every prediction Groundswell makes is stored, then graded against what actually happened — direction, size, timing — and the running track record is public. When the model is wrong, the site says so. That one constraint shaped the data pipeline, how forecasts are versioned, and what the interface is even allowed to claim.

steps.label: The hard part
steps.body: Publishing your own error rate is a trust asset and a marketing liability at the same time. A competitor who never grades itself will always _look_ more confident. The wager is that a certain kind of surfer would rather have an honest tool than a slick one — and that betting the product on that is worth the people it turns away.

steps.label: Where it stands
steps.body: Live for 600+ spots in five languages, backed by four-plus years of historical data, running as an installable PWA. It has a real, if still small, group of people who check it before they paddle out — not a paying base yet, but genuine repeat use, which is the signal that counts at this stage. The open question now is turning honest utility into something people pay for without compromising the thing that makes it honest.

I am committed to building applications that meet **WAI WCAG 2.1**, **Section 508**, and **ADA** standards for accessibility. My goal is to ensure that every product I design or develop can be used effectively by all people — regardless of ability or device.

This site is held to that standard. Every page is checked against **WCAG 2.1 AA** with axe-core — the same audit engine behind [AccessBridge](https://accessbridge.app), my accessibility-scanning tool — and the current build reports **zero automated violations** across all routes, the keyboard-shortcuts dialog included.
